speechtext: Pursuant to the Order made Tuesday, April 16, 1985, the House will now proceed to hear statements with regard to the Charter of Rights equality provisions.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the Government of Canada to celebrate the coming into effect of the equality rights provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As of today the Constitution of Canada guarantees that every individual in Canada is equal before and under the law, and has the right to equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age, or mental or physical disability.
This is an important milestone in the evolution of Canada and Canadian values. It is furthermore the constitutional extension of the 1960 Bill of Rights championed by the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker and which formed an important part of the Progressive Conservative record of concern for and commitment to human rights and fundamental freedoms.

Hon. Members will no doubt recall that during the historic debate in Parliament on the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, our Party made every effort to have Canadians from all walks of life participate in the proceedings of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution.
Equality rights, which from now on are enshrined in our Constitution, enjoy the support of Canadians in every part of this country and the support of all the parties represented in this House.
The coming into effect of the provisions of Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is for Canada an important step towards the full recognition and broad application of equality rights. That does not mean that our work is done. Today, we are being asked to start a new phase.

The attainment of equality is an evolving process. It is not always easy to make adjustments to the complex inheritance of the past in order to accommodate changing values. It is for this reason that the coming into effect of Section 15 was delayed for three years, so that Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the Provinces and Territories could bring about conformity between current laws and policies and the requirements of the equality provisions of the Charter.
This required that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) review over 1,100 federal statutes, an unprecedented task. As a result of this review, the Minister introduced the first Charter Compliance Bill in the House of Commons on January 31 of this year. Published at the same time was a discussion paper on equality issues in federal laws. A special subcommittee of this House has been established to examine this paper and to consult with Canadians. The work of this Committee will be vital in ensuring the conformity of our laws with the equality provisions of the Charter. One such further change is now before the House. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) has introduced Bill C-31 to remove sexual discrimination from the Indian Act. [Translation]
However, I must point out that it is not enough to review certain rights and to eliminate certain legal obstacles to equality. We must also, where necessary, adopt a new attitude and modify our policies, programs and practices.
In certain areas, it will be necessary to take measures for affirmative action or social development, in order to correct the inequities resulting from various forms of discrimination practised in the past.

In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I want to reiterate solemnly the commitment of the Government to pursue meaningful equality. Since we took office we have acted as vigorously and as expeditiously as possible to honour this commitment. That is why the Government adopted a dynamic approach to selfgovernment for aboriginal peoples. That is why, in our response to the Abella Report, we accepted the concept of employment equity. That is why we are moving to implement the Obstacles report respecting the disabled, and that is why government commitments arising from the Equality Now! report on visible minorities are being fulfilled.
Hon. Members will no doubt recall the following words from the November 5 Speech from the Throne:
As the women of Canada know, there is some distance between the principle of equality, widely accepted, and its reality, still far short of achievement.
We are acting as quickly as possible to close this gap. Since this Government took office the number of women in Cabinet has risen to the highest level ever, and the percentage of Order in Council appointments held by women has risen from 15 to 22 per cent-a substantial increase in a brief period of time, but one that will be improved upon continually.

April 17, 1985
Charter of Rights

Parliament and the Government of Canada will have a duty to help Canadians progress towards full compliance with equality rights, both in our legislation and in practice. It was in that perspective that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) recently announced the very substantial grants to be made to the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and the Coalition of Provincial Organizations for the Disabled.
I said earlier that the event we celebrate today is not the end of a process but an important watershed, an opportunity for a new beginning. In the area of human rights, Canada has a record of which it can be proud, and the capacity to do even better and thus serve as a model society for others to emulate.
Creating an open, free, and egalitarian society, however, requires more than constitutional provisions, sound laws, and effective government programs. It requires a deep and abiding sense of fairness on the part of all Canadians. It is within our reach as a people to ensure that all our acts are guided by generosity and tolerance, fraternity and understanding.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, today is a great day for all Canadians as a result of the coming into force of the equality rights Section of the Charter. As a Liberal, I am proud that my Party fought long and hard not only to patriate the Constitution but also to include in the Constitution a Charter of Rights and Freedoms which is of fundamental importance to all Canadians.
The history of mankind has been the struggle of civilized people against the forces od darkness and evil to defend the rights, liberties, and dignities of their fellow human beings. In a global sense we are all part of a minority, and thus subject to the tyranny of the majority. If we are not protected by the rule of the law which is embedded in the rock of our Constitution, what is left?
Today equality becomes not merely protected by law; it becomes the very foundation stone upon which all laws must either stand or fall. But we cannot rely only on laws and courts to end discrimination in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we have come a very long way since 1867. Perhaps all the values we have acquired in this country over the past 118 years may be summed up today as we formally acknowledge that all citizens are equal before the law in Canada, that there are no longer any second-class citizens in our society, and that our land no longer harbours people who cannot clearly express their religious, cultural and linguistic differences, while at the same time standing as proud citizens of the country which is perhaps the freest in the world.
The progress we have made in this House in recent years as a result of the new Constitution ranks us among the world's
leading countries, but even though we do have today a constitutional statute under which all citizens enjoy rights, it is imperative that Canadians too adopt a new attitude. Generosity, tolerance, understanding and frankness must become national virtues. We must be able to show respect for every region of this country, for every individual in our society, because when we travel we find out that Canada is known the world over as a country which has shown that building a great nation in such a diversified world is not an impossible endeavour. Canada stands for two official languages and comprises a myriad of religious groups. It is also home to different cultural communities, yet more and more we realize that no matter where one may be, from British Columbia to Newfoundland, one can rest assured that one's francophone fellow Canadians are respected, that if one is a Quebecer, one knows that women, the handicapped and the elderly are treated with equality in our society.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that all Hon. Members of the House are justified in rejoicing today. Of course, this achievement did not come about without difficulty.
We have had a lot of fights over these things. A lot of speeches were made; there was a lot of emotion, and a lot of delays. But today, whoever is in this House who was here some years ago, will realize that out of the struggle of the mind and the spirit of this House came the equality rights which guarantee that all Canadians are equal. For that, Canada is a better country. I hope that all Canadians will apply the virtue of the equality clause in their daily lives. It is for all Canadians an achievement of greatness. Canada is the land of opportunity, the land of equality, and the land of tolerance par excellence.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, there can be few days more significant in the history of a nation than today, the day upon which Section 15, the equality rights Section of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, comes into effect.
The NDP, and the CCF before it, have always solidly supported the concept of an effectively entrenched Charter of Rights without the possibility of override. Indeed, it was a distinguished lawyer and former judge, Thomas Berger, who perhaps put it best in his book Fragile Freedoms, when he wrote:
Judges may not always be wiser than politicians, but they should be able to stand more firmly against angry winds blowing in the streets.
Therefore, today should be a day for rejoicing and celebrating, particularly by those groups which have been most affected by decades of inequality, be they women's groups or minorities.
The passage of the Constitution three years ago gave rise to tremendous hopes and expectations by millions of Canadians that Governments, both federal and provincial, would take
April 17, 1985

seriously their obligations to amend legislation to bring it into compliance with the provisions of the Charter.

I am sure that we all deeply regret the fact that the Province of Quebec was not signatory to the constitutional agreement. That is why Quebec chose to avail itself of the notwithstanding clause in Section 33 of the Charter, with the result that Quebecers are being denied important rights under the Charter, including equality rights under Section 15. We all hope that, before too long, a new formula will be found to enable six million Quebecers to become full-fledged participants under the terms of the Constitution of Canada.

What should have been a day of rejoicing and celebrating is instead, unfortunately, also tinged with a sense of anger and betrayal-betrayal of the hopes and dreams of women and minorities for real legislative change, and anger that Governments have not yet made a reality of the promise of full equality. Three years have passed, many studies have been done, and there is still no legislation of substance to implement real equality.
How can we possibly explain to two million disabled Canadians that the only change in laws affecting them was a change in the wording in the Canada Shipping Act, which changed the word "lunacy" to the words "mental disability"? How do we defend before Canadian women, who fought with incredible energy and strength for real and meaningful equality and who continue to be the victims of discrimination at home and at work, the failure of Governments to make long overdue changes in areas such as pension legislation and unemployment insurance provisions? Can we really say there exists full equality in Canada when five women lost their jobs in the Canadian Armed Forces solely on the basis of sexual orientation? The inaction of Governments means that women and minorities will be forced into the courts to define and defend their rights.
Despite the promises by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) during the election campaign to provide financial assistance for important litigation under the equality rights Section of the Charter of Rights, no funding announcement has been made so far. Declarations of rights, without adequate enforcement mechanisms, make a mockery of the concept of full equality. As Frank Scott said so eloquently:
The trappings of democracy hang loosely on an emaciated body politic.
As the role of the judiciary is significantly enhanced and strengthened, the time has come to make fundamental changes to the way in which judges are appointed, to ensure an independent and outstanding bench, with far more women and minorities represented-judges who display sensitivity to the complex and often novel rights issues which are raised in the context of the Charter of Rights.
Let us take this opportunity, on the date of the coming into force of the equality rights Section, to rededicate ourselves as parliamentarians and Canadians to the creation of full equality for all in Canada, using strong affirmative action where
necessary. Let us not wait for the courts to speak but rather let us move forward now to make that promise of equality, received with such hope and such optimism in 1982, a reality in 1985.

PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF ELLEN FAIRCLOUGH, RENAUDE LAPOINTE, AND GRACE MacINNIS

Out of respect for the day, and respect for their contributions to this day, may I signal the presence in our gallery of three distinguised Canadian parliamentarians; the Hon. Ellen Fairclough, the Hon. Senator Renaude Lapointe, and Mrs. Grace Maclnnis.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-UNITED KINGDOM PUBLIC OPINION POLL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just learned that an opinion poll was published in Britain this morning on the attitude of the British public toward acid rain. The poll found that 55 per cent of the British people are prepared to pay the additional hydro costs which would be incurred by the United Kingdom if they were to join the 30 per cent club initiated by Canada in March, 1984, when ten like-minded nations committed themselves to a 30 per cent reduction of S02 emissions by 1983.
There are now 20 nations, including Canada, which have joined the 30 per cent club, but seven European countries, namely, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Greece, Yugoslavia, and Turkey, have still to join. The United Kingdom is responsible for the creation of European acid rain in the amount of 4 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide annually, or one-fifth of western Europe's total. This opinion poll demonstrates significant public awareness of the problems concerning acid rain.
I am sure that Hon. Members of this House, and Canadians at large, welcome the news that the British public supports the need for action on acid rain. In addition, we hope that this poll will motivate the British Government to join the 30 per cent club and become a signatory of the Helsinki Agreement in July of this year. This, for us in Canada, would be a desirable development because we will then be looking south to the United States Government to follow suit-

April 17, 1985

Mr. Speaker, in this morning's The Globe and Mail, the Prime Minister's Office boasted about the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) has kept an earlier promise to pay for his family's food bills. We are informed that he wrote a cheque for $4,000 covering the period from September 17, 1984, to March 31, 1985. Canadians should take a close look at these figures because, if they do, they will be surprised at what they discover. If you cover the 170-day period and multiply it by three meals a day for the five-person Mulroney family, you will generate a total of 2,550 meals over this period-
Oh, oh!
Tell us what Trudeau did.

Accordingly, when one divides the $4,000 by the amount of meals consumed, the average cost of the Mulroney meal, per person, is $1.50. The Prime Minister is certainly the winner of today's "The Price is Right" game. A coffee and a bologna sandwich cost more. This even beats the parliamentary cafeteria prices which the Prime Minister complained about only months ago. 1 ask you, Mr. Speaker, what average Canadian family pays as little as $1.50 per meal? The attempt of the Prime Minister to be perceived as paying his way is a complete sham, and it underestimates people's intelligence. He should fully honour his earlier commitment and not play his familiar deception game.
Shame!
The Prime Minister's latest food for thought to Canadians is insulting. His menu is completely unappetizing and distasteful-
1 regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the women of Canada join all Canadians in celebrating the enactment of the equality Section of the Charter of Rights. I salute the many talented and determined women who came together in 1982 in the ad hoc committee to educate, lobby, formulate, and demand inclusion of Sections 15 and 28 in our Charter of Rights. Their efforts, supported by women parliamentarians, overcame many obstacles to achieve the beginnings of equality. But this is only a beginning. Unfortunately, Governments have
not amended legislation to conform to Charter requirements. As a result, women, native people, the disabled, and other minority groups will be forced to fight for their rights through skilful lobbying, negotiations and litigation.
1 urge the Government, on this momentous day, to prove its commitment to Section 15 by contributing to an independent, non-political endowment being established for legal action. We will truly celebrate equality when women have equal opportunities for full employment, equal pay for work of equal value, paid parental leave, universal day care, reproductive choice, and an end to violence and poverty in all our communities.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to rise in the House on the very day that Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms becomes effective.
Section 15 contains only two sentences, but those two sentences enshrine equality rights for all Canadians in the Canadian Constitution. Furthermore, Section 15 affirms the legal right of Canadian women to full equality with their male counterparts in all areas of our society.
Mr. Speaker, I think the fact that this section becomes effective this year is particularly significant, since 1985 marks the end of the United Nations decade for women, and Canada has taken an active part in all the activities organized around this decade.
We can be proud of what we have accomplished during the past ten years in promoting the rights of Canadian women and improving the status of women throughout the world.
Furthermore, on November 5, the Federal Government made a firm commitment in the Speech from the Throne to close the gap that exists between the principle of equality and its application. Legislation has already been tabled in the House to respond to women's needs, and today, Mr. Speaker, the Charter has launched a major challenge to Canadian men and women. subtopic: TRIBUTE TO WOMEN'S INTEREST IN CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM
TRIBUTE TO WOMEN'S INTEREST IN CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the third anniversary of the coming into effect of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but it will be today, April 17, 1985, that will be recorded in history as the day the Charter truly came into effect, for what is a Charter of Rights and Freedoms without guarantees of equality?
Today I want to pay special tribute to Canadian women who took a special interest in constitutional reform. They took the issue of equality rights and made it their personal cause. Because of their investment of time, energy, and hope, it is paying off for all of us today. Later today many of those women will join together in Room 200 of the West Block, a room of historic significance, where the Constitutional Committee held its hearings and where the ad hoc women's meetings were held in February, 1981.
Tonight we shall remember the dedication of the women of the past, women such as Nellie McClung and Agnes McPhail, who pioneered equality for women in Canada. We shall honour the women of today who played such an important role in ensuring the inclusion of equality provisions for women in the Charter, who shall continue that determined struggle in their presentations to our parliamentary committee on equality rights, and before the courts with the help of the legal education and action fund.
Finally, tonight we shall pause for a moment in anticipation of the success of the women of the future, your daughters and mine, who can grow and prosper in a country and society which respect differences but demand equality-

ANGUS MacINNIS'S DEFENCE OF JAPANESE CANADIANS IN 1941

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), and other Members who saw the exchange yesterday in this House on the subject of Canadians of Japanese origin, to these words spoken in this House on February 25, 1941, by Angus Mac-Innis, the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, and I quote:
If we are to have harmonious and friendly relations between the oriental population and the rest of our British Columbia citizens, we must stop discriminating against and abusing the orientals. We must find some common ground on which we can work, and I think it can be found ... I am satisfied that if we treat the Japanese and our other oriental citizens right, we shall get their loyalty, because they are no longer orientals in the accepted sense of that term. They would feel as much out of place in Japan as we would. I know them, speak to them; I visit them and have them in my home, and I have not the slightest doubt that what I say is correct. If we are to avoid the troubles that other
countries have had with racial minorities, then we must take a realistic view of the situation in British Columbia and attempt to make these people feel at home among us. We will secure their loyalty by fairness and kindness and by the practice of those other attributes which we exercise in our relations with other people.
Let us evoke that spirit and have genuine negotiations for an apology and appropriate compensation to Canadians of Japanese origin.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Sub-committee on Rights and Freedoms, 1 welcome this opportunity today to comment on Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The work performed by the Sub-committee will give the people of Canada a chance to shape and influence the practical applications of these fundamental rights and freedoms. These will include equality before the law, equality under the law, and equal protection and benefit of the law.

Today we celebrate the entrenchment of equality rights in the Charter. The implementation of this clause signals a commitment by Governments to move at full speed toward the goal of full equality for all Canadians. This is a date with equality. All individuals are now guaranteed equality, not as a right to be acquired but as a state that exists, not just in the laws themselves, but also in their administration. From this day on all Canadians can be assured that the Government's commitment to equality is more than an enunciation of principle. It has become the instrument to address actively injustices that have prevailed far too long.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF RESPECT FOR RIGHT TO BE DIFFERENT
IMPORTANCE OF RESPECT FOR RIGHT TO BE DIFFERENT
speechtext:
As equality rights committee co-chairman, Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss indeed were I to remain silent on this day, April 17, 1985, a milestone in the evolution of all Canadian men and women. Unfortunately, this kind of evolution does have ups and downs, so our Government took the initiative of establishing this equality rights committee.
May all Canadians, men and women alike, make the best of this consultation process to pursue the debate which began a long time ago and which must go on until our institutions, our policies, our commitments, our actions and our attitudes fully reflect not so much the right to equality as respect for the right to be different.
Mr. Speaker, on this day when Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms Section 15 comes into effect, let us hope that our conception of human rights will encourage Canadian men and women to fulfil their aspirations.

Mr. Speaker, today is the fiftieth anniversary of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration. It was on April 17, 1935, that Royal Assent was given to the Act setting up the agency that did so much to rescue the Prairies from a crisis of drought and soil erosion. This agency, a vital part of the federal Agriculture Department, is still hard at work at soil and water conservation on the Prairies. A great deal has been done, but much remains to be done.
Our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) recognizes soil erosion as a most serious problem facing Canadian agriculture today, second only to farm financing. The future demands a
great deal more public awareness of the need to conserve our soils, not only on the Prairies but throughout Canada. Farmers lose significantly when the quality of their soil deteriorates. When soil is blowing or washing away, money is always lost.
A public education program could help the PFRA, other public and private organizations and, most important, the farmers of Canada, to build on the past and increase their efforts to preserve and protect our threatened soils.

subsubtopic: RADIO STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. As I said earlier, today is a great day for all Canadians with the coming into effect of the equality clause in the Constitution. I presume that the Prime Minister agrees with the generous statement made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration about Section 15 and what it means for Canada. I only hope that the Minister of Justice, whose job it is to uphold our Constitution, will agree.
Does the Prime Minister agree with the very sad and very wrong comment of the Minister of Justice in a CBC radio interview this morning, in which the Minister said: "It is too bad that the Constitution allows courts to determine what constitutes discrimination"? Will the Prime Minister tell his Minister of Justice that the Constitution is supposed to protect minorities from the abuse of the majority, if necessary, through the courts? Will the Prime Minister tell his Minister of Justice that we would have a lot less court cases if the Government would start making changes in our laws now so that Canadians will not have to go to court to fight for their rights?

Oral Questions THE ECONOMY

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance I will direct my question to the Acting Minister of Finance. Yesterday the Minister of Finance said that as a result of the Government's upcoming Budget, Canadians should expect the inflation rate to go up. In doing so, the Minister is fuelling inflationary expectations. By musing out loud, the Minister is personally making inflation worse at the time when the Government may decide to de-index certain social programs. Why does the Government want to introduce policies that will fuel inflation and damage the buying power of low and middle-income Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is obviously making inferences from the statement. Let me underline the fact that in the last three months the inflation rate has been 3.7 per cent. It is a record with which we are pleased and quite happy to have achieved.
I would only reassure the Hon. Member that the policies that will be introduced by this Government will be directed toward maintaining a level of inflation that is low and acceptable to all Canadians.
I am amazed that the Acting Minister of Linance is talking about anti-inflation measures. The fact is that it is the six and five measure that really brought inflation down.

It is common knowledge that energy prices are a very important element in the consumer price index. After having given away $2.4 billion to the oil multinationals, is the Government prepared to increase gas taxes at the pump so that the real reason for inflation rising will depend on the taxes imposed by the Government?

However, I think that the government intends, as stated by the Minister of Finance, to establish policies aimed at keeping the

subsubtopic: LITIGATION BY THE DISABLED AND THE HANDICAPPED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. There is wide recognition that many claims under the Charter will be required by necessity to go before the courts for a resolution, to be brought by many women's groups, organizations of the disabled, and many visible minority groups. Do the Prime Minister and the Government continue to stand by their commitment which they made to the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped on August 14 last, to establish a rights and freedom defence fund, when he wrote to that organization and said: "A Progressive Conservative Government will financially assist all Charter of Rights cases deemed to be of national importance"?

subsubtopic: LITIGATION BY THE DISABLED AND THE HANDICAPPED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been no change in the Government's position. The question of court challenges and funding appears to presume a failure of the legislatures of Canada to bring existing laws in line with the Charter.
We are committed as a Government, and as a political Party we are no less committed than the NDP. I suppose that if there were a special area of responsibility-all areas are deserving-it would be with regard to the handicapped. 1 can assure you that we will not flag in our determination to ensure justice and fairness for those who deserve it under the Charter.

Mr. Speaker, specifically, could the Prime Minister assure the House that any claims brought before the courts by disability organizations, women's groups, or visible minorities, that those cases will receive the financial support of the Government, because there is absolutely no question that they will be very expensive?

Mr. Speaker, I ask the Hon. Member to reflect for a moment on the possible significance of that question. As I understood it, the Hon. Member is not asking me to ensure that worthy and deserving causes of those who perhaps, lack the necessary resources, are placed in a position where they can bring worthy litigation forward. The Hon. Member appears to be asking whether the Government of Canada will not fund, willy-nilly, holus-bolus, every conceivable challenge that will be brought under the statutes.
He is not asking that.
Now the leader of the Ian Deans club says he is not asking that.
No, he is not. You know what he is asking. You can't obfuscate.

I will go back and look at the question as asked. If I am wrong, I will apologize to my hon. friend.
The question, as I understood it, seemed to imply an absolutely impossible situation of impending litigation. Our situation is that in those areas where the Government of Canada can and should act to be helpful in ensuring that litigants are capable of exercising their rights before the law, and they are in any way precluded from doing so, we shall act.
I cannot give a guarantee that we will finance every case that arises in every conceivable manner against every conceivable cause, under the Charter.

Mr. Speaker, since that was not the question I asked, will the Prime Minister advise the House whether the Government of Canada intends to establish a fund that will be of assistance to groups who cannot afford to go through the courts on their own, so that they can effectively fight for their rights before the courts? I am talking about a fund, not specific cases, but a central fund that groups can draw upon?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that it was one of the amendments put forward by the Progressive Conservative Party that ensured the creation of such funds to ensure that certain groups would be able to bring forward their rights. I salute my colleagues and those other Members of the House who supported that amendment at the time. I think it was extremely worth while, and we shall honour it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Ninety per cent of workers are covered under provincial, not federal law. At the current rate of salary catch-up, Canadian women can expect equal pay with Canadian men in 97 years. Has the Prime Minister received assurances from the provinces that all Canadian women will be protected by the introduction of equal pay for work of equal value laws in every province?

No, Mr. Speaker, I have not received such assurances. I committed the Party and the Government to placing that question, and others involving dignity and equal opportunity for women, at the head of the list in terms of the premiers' conference in Regina, and I did precisely that. It remains a key item of all federal-provincial negotiations. This Party is deeply committed to that
April 17, 1985

spirit of fairness and justice. I know the Hon. Member will be supportive of me and the Government as we proceed in this vital area of fairness to women.

Mr. Speaker, in light of the importance of this issue, will the Prime Minister immediately call a First Ministers' conference on employment equity, or is he prepared to leave the question to people like the Premier of Ontario who is so out of touch with Canadian women-
Oh, oh!
-that when he was Treasurer he introduced a tax on tampons as a non-essential item?

May I say
with respect, Mr. Speaker, that I am somewhat dismayed that on a day of such importance to women the object of the exercise would be clearly to score some cheap political points on behalf of the Liberal Party of Ontario. The Hon. Member inelegantly bailed out of the Liberal Party in opposition in Ontario, to wind up in an equally inelegant position here in Ottawa. We are here to defend and protect the rights of women. We want the advancement of women across the country, and that kind of attitude does not help.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: DEPICTION OF INDIANS IN DEPARTMENTAL PAMPHLET
DEPICTION OF INDIANS IN DEPARTMENTAL PAMPHLET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Hon. Secretary of State. Unfortunately the Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not protect aboriginal peoples against any biased and distorted version of history, particularly when it is in a government publication. The 1985 Canada Day application form, A Salute to Youth, says that colonists represent the youth of Canada's past, but it makes no mention of the fact that aboriginal peoples were here before.
Is the Minister aware that Indians are pictured as the enemy of Canadian youth when the pamphlet tells about a 15 year old girl, Madeleine de Vercheres, who fought against Indian attacks for eight days to save her family seigneury? Was the Minister aware of these distortions? Will he withdraw this pamphlet, and will he apologize to the Indian, Inuit, and Metis people of Canada for this biased and unfair version of their history?

subtopic: DEPICTION OF INDIANS IN DEPARTMENTAL PAMPHLET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the Hon. Member, I will certainly look at the document. I was not aware of that, but I will look at it. However, let me make this assertion to the Hon. Member. He may choose to pick one area which is an illustration of the whole question of stereotyping that affects not only women but many of our visible minorities and our native people. Part of
Oral Questions
the citizenship directory responsibility of the Secretary of State's Department is to tackle this, and to work along with Canada's indigenous group in order that together we can carry out community education. Today's celebrations are a part of that over-all sensitizing of the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the Minister will first of all attack this in his own Department with the people who are responsible for this kind of publication.
Does the Minister recognize that this type of stereotyped version of Canadian history has given false justification to our past denial of aboriginal rights, and that it is still operative in the case of Premiers such as Devine, Lougheed and Bennett? 1 ask him to look closely at this. What action is he prepared to take to ensure that a balanced view of Canadian history is given to Canadians so that we understand the basis of aboriginal rights?

Mr. Speaker, whatever the faults of my Department may be, one of them is not insensitivity in this area. There are committed men and women who are sensitive to this and are doing their best across the country to provide that type of education. I think the Hon. Member will agree that at the First Ministers' conference there was a further illustration of the sincerity of the Government to deal effectively with Canada's first peoples.

Mr. Speaker, my question to the Prime Minister deals with the systemic discrimination against women, that is, unintentional discrimination through the application of legislation and regulations. An increasing number of people concerned with equality in employment agree that this systemic discrimination remains one of the major obstacles to employment not only for women, but for native peoples, the visible minorities and the handicapped as well. Does the Prime Minister recognize that there is such a thing as systemic discrimination?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised a most important issue. There is in our economy a built-in and progressive discrimination which victimizes women. There is for instance the so-called technological breakthrough which, by the end of this decade, will jeopardize over one million jobs held by women in the service industry, a far greater number than in the case of men. I can understand the hon. member's concern and, together with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, I have

April 17, 1985
Oral Questions
already taken some serious initiatives in the hope of reaching an agreement in order to improve the lot of the many women who are caught in this unfortunate and unfair predicament. I am grateful to the hon. member for raising this issue of vital importance for both Canadian men and women.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that the Prime Minister apparently realizes the existence of discrimination within the system. This is by far the best kept secret in the marketplace.
Elowever, I have a second question: In order to provide these groups with greater protection against this type of discrimina-ton and against poverty, would the Prime Minister commit himself today to take the necessary remedial action and advise the House as to exactly when he intends to do so?

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Member that we had already taken a number of initiatives while in the opposition, because my colleagues and I had experienced in the private sector the well-founded claims the hon. member is making. Yes, we will indeed be faced within the foreseeable future with a human tragedy of major proportion. We have already implemented a number of manpower retraining schemes, created many new openings within small- and medium-size businesses to benefit women mostly, in order to do something useful and hopefully solve this problem. This is not something that can be done overnight, but I think we have taken a number of steps in the right direction and eventually will solve this most serious problem.

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to ask a question of the Minister of the Environment about whether, in light of the PCB spill, she intended to reinstate the four or five programs concerning research into the effects of PCBs, which were cancelled. However, she is not here again today, for the second time, and my question is directed to either the Minister of Transport or the Prime Minister, whomever would clear up the question of federal responsibility as it affects this PCB spill.
We have the Minister of the Environment announcing regulations which properly come under the Minister of Transport. Would the Prime Minister or the Minister of Transport indicate, if indeed there is a federal responsibility in this area, as I believe there is, why there is no one on the scene from Environment Canada; no one on the scene from the Canadian Transport Commission, Dangerous Goods Division; and only one person on the scene from Transport Canada, who is there
for a purely technical assessment of the transformer which leaked? We had an announcement this morning having to do with regulations that will affect this kind of incident. Why do we have no federal people on the scene to speak of, except the one I mentioned?

Mr. Speaker, first I want to inform the House that the Minister of the Environment is in Burlington and Toronto for two very full days of meetings with respect to acid rain and toxic materials. These are long standing commitments. I think the Hon. Member will recognize this is an obligation on her part to honour that invitation.
With respect to the other part of the question, within less than two hours of the incident, the Canutec organization of Transport Canada was informed. There has been collaboration on an ongoing basis. There is a representative on site. There has been collaboration with the federal Department of the Environment. We are working very closely together. The investigation is being spearheaded by the Ontario Department of the Environment, but in very close collaboration with both federal Departments. The Hon. Member should recognize that we recognize the gravity of the situation and are working very closely with the Department of the Environment of Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, it is hard to get the impression of the gravity with which the Government considers this matter when the first person to arrive on the scene federally arrived this morning, not two hours but four days after the event. There is still no one on the scene from Environment Canada or the CTC. When will the Government take its responsibility, not just in this instance but in the over-all, ensuring that there is a federal responsibility in this area, not just by announcing regulations for July 1, but by stepping in and not relying on the Ontario Government to do this, and claiming a federal responsibility for preventing these kinds of incidents?

Mr. Speaker, I repeat once again that the Province of Ontario has primary jurisdiction over this matter. It has taken the leadership role. The federal Departments of Transport and the Environment are collaborating and working together very closely. We will take whatever corrective action is necessary. We are now exploring the possibility of providing for a protection directive under Section 28 of the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to my hon. friend, the Acting Minister of the Environment. I want the Minister to know that the people of northern Ontario are frightened and are very
April 17, 1985

angry about the recent PCB spillage. Quite frankly, we have had enough. We have had mercury in the water, we have acid rain, and now we have a PCB spillage on the Trans-Canada Highway. The people of northern Ontario feel betrayed by this Government and by the Government of Ontario. What can the Minister tell us today to assure us that the Trans-Canada Highway is not going to become a path of poison?

speakeroldname: Hon. John A. Fraser (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand the Hon. Member rising here on behalf of people in his constituency and expressing, as is appropriate, the outrage and dismay that follow for all decent Canadians as a result of this incident. It is a very serious one. However, I have to say in response, as I said yesterday, that there is mixed jurisdiction in this. The federal Government is coming in with new regulations in July. One can say that they should have been here before. One can also say that perhaps somebody who was here before should have passed them.
People are on the site, and were on the site immediately. This is not a situation where no one did anything. You can ask federal legislators or federal administrators to go there, but in fact in practical terms the responsibility for looking after the traffic, assessing the damage, and doing something about the clean-up, happens to be with Ministry of the Environment of the Province of Ontario. That is our system, and there is nothing wrong with that. I say to the Hon. Member that the federal Government takes this matter very seriously. I would ask the Hon. Member to convey that very clearly to the people that he represents, and represents so adequately.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents are tired of hearing about jurisdiction, responsibility, guidelines, and regulations. They feel that this Government and the Government of Ontario have betrayed them. PCBs were spilled. How can we be assured that this will not happen again, that there will not be another failure? What action does the Minister propose? People in northern Ontario want to know that this kind of avoidable accident will never happen again.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the transportation of dangerous goods, particularly the transportation of dangerous substances, our departmental officials are currently exploring the possibility of a protection directive under the provisions of the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, Section 28, which may be implemented. It would provide for a kind of regulatory control and/or moratorium on the transportation of these substances. That is being looked into. If it is necessary to move in that direction, this Government will move in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to return to the Minister of Transport. It would appear that there is nobody in charge of this matter. Do the Minister of Trans-
Ora/ Questions
port and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans not know that interprovincial and international trucking under the Constitution of Canada are totally the responsibility of the federal Government? Is it not correct that the Minister of Transport has allowed provincial Departments to move in and, as a result, there is a hodge-podge? Will the Minister agree that it is time for him to exercise the constitutional authority he has over interprovincial trucking, particularly in the case of the transportation of dangerous goods?

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised at the Hon. Member, given his experience in the field of transportation. He should know better than to make the statement that he did. Truck transportation, both intra and extra-provincial, is a provincial matter. The Hon. Member can shake his head in the negative, but he knows darn well that that is the case. Under the transportation of dangerous goods regulations, and the need to promulgate regulations, that is exactly where the difficulty has arisen because there needs to be the capability and the cohesiveness of a regulatory system right across the country. We have been working with the provinces, trying to work out that kind of uniform system. On July 1 these regulations will be in effect. Having said that, there still is a code with respect to the handling and the manufacturing of these substances which is provided for by the Department of the Environment which is being followed.
Order, please.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. The Minister of Transport knows perfectly well that the jurisdiction of the Government of Canada has been abrogated by the provinces. He still has the constitutional authority on interprovincial and international trucking. Because nobody is in charge, will the Minister take charge (a) on the investigation and (b), if he will not go for a moratorium on movements between now and July 1, will he ensure that any transportation of dangerous goods is convoyed, with inspections at least every 50 miles? Will he do that under the constitutional authority that he has under the Constitution of Canada and the National Transportation Act?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the New Democratic Party came very close to asking for a moratorium on the movement of all dangerous goods in Canada. The Member is now backing off. That would have even included farm chemicals, and the farmers might not get in a crop this year. I have indicated that the federal Departments of Transport and the Environment are very closely involved with the Department of the Environment of the Province of Ontario in monitoring and assessing this situation and investigating the accident. I said earlier that we are exploring the possibilities of providing for a protection directive under Section 28 of the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act which could have the effect of meeting the request

April 17, 1985
Oral Questions
that the Hon. Member has submitted to the House this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, today is a very special and important day in the history of Canada as the Charter of Rights and Freedoms becomes law. My question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. There exists today within the Armed Forces a situation that blatantly discriminates against pregnant service personnel who must take leave without pay or use vacation time during their time of confinement. What action will the Minister take to redress this discrimination that exists within his Department and to bring the Armed Forces into line with the non-discriminatory provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I believe the Hon. Member is aware, regulations now exist in the Armed Forces accommodating the pregnancies of female personnel. It may well be that there are some deficiencies in those regulations. I have asked for an analysis and careful study to be done, and of course, at the same time, under Section 15, the Subcommittee of the Justice and Legal Affairs Standing Committee will undoubtedly be inquiring into these areas in its studies of the reference made to that committee by the Minister of Justice.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT EQUALITY-COMPLIANCE BY COMPANIES CONTRACTING WITH GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It is not enough, of course, to give lip service today to equality. In the spirit of the Charter of Rights and to bring about employment equity, the Special Parliamentary Committee on the Disabled of the previous Liberal Government recommended that private sector companies doing more than $20,000 worth of business with the Government be required to take affirmative action and hire the handicapped. The Prime Minister, during the election campaign, assured handicapped persons that he would support this measure. However, in her recent reply to the Abella report, the Minister of Employment and Immigration only requires compliance by companies receiving contracts worth over $200,000. How can the Minister shortchange disabled and handicapped people in this way by leaving out thousands upon thousands of companies from compliance?

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT EQUALITY-COMPLIANCE BY COMPANIES CONTRACTING WITH GOVERNMENT

We figured that 85 per cent, although not totally inclusive, is nevertheless a good beginning, and we will see that those measures are put in place so that there is equality for those persons who are handicapped, for visible minorities, for native groups, and for women.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Minister knows that a contract for $1 million can be let through five contracts worth $200,000 each and the companies would be exempt. I am amazed that she would say what she has said. Nevertheless, since the Minister of Employment and Immigration said that people in business who have already adopted employment equity have seen substantial growth in their productivity, profits, and people, why did she not give this wonderful opportunity to all companies that receive contracts worth $20,000 and allow them to enjoy these benefits which she herself has outlined?

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my response I said that we were taking a first step. I think it is an important and very valuable first step. It is a first step, however, because we are at the beginning of a process. Had the previous Government thought it was worth while to do anything at all in this field, the women of Canada, the disabled, the native people, and the visible minorities would have been much further along the road. We are overcoming those obstacles. I trust the Hon. Member will give the provisions we have introduced the support they merit.

Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Agriculture. Is the Minister aware that this spring, prairie farmers will face the possibility of the worst grasshopper outbreak in several decades? Will the Minister inform the House of what steps his Department is taking to join with provincial Governments in preparing for that outbreak?
Well, spray them with PCBs.

Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the Hon. Member that I am aware of and deeply concerned over the potential outbreak of grasshopper infestations in western Canada during the 1985 season. According to surveys done in the latter part of 1984, the potential is much greater in Alberta and Saskatchewan. In the Hon. Member's home province of Manitoba, the possibility
April 17, 1985

may be that the infestation there might well exceed the 1984 infestation by two and a half times.
I would like to assure the Hon. Member that our researchers and scientists throughout the network of research stations in western Canada are working in consultation and co-operation with the provincial Governments and the producer organizations. We have an alert system in place, and we will be able to inform producers of the day-to-day situation with respect to grasshopper infestations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The very distinguished former Under-Secretary of State, George Ball, has written a devastating critique of star wars in this week's The New York Review of Books. Perhaps the Prime Minister may have seen it. It describes star wars as being deceptive, confused, and ill-considered, and as undermining deterrence and threatening to escalate the arms race to an unmanageable spiral. Has the Prime Minister read Mr. Ball's critique? Has he been listening to the concerns of ordinary Canadians, including those in the peace camp outside this building, about the devastating implications of star wars? If so, why has the Canadian Government not yet given an emphatic no to the whole concept of star wars, and an emphatic no to any Canadian participation in it whatsoever?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her question. As the only Party Leader to be present in the House of Commons on such an important day for women, I want to thank her as well for her contribution to the progress that has been made.
In point of fact, I did see the review written by Mr. Ball. He is a man of considerable reputation. The Hon. Member will recall that he held an important position in the U.S. administration. Mr. Ball held an important position in the administration when it was involved in Vietnam. He held certain views then that have not been borne out over the years. He now holds this view. I respect him for his analysis and for his point of view. I can tell the Hon. Member that it is not shared by our NATO allies. It is not shared by the Secretary-General of NATO. However, it is a view, and Mr. Ball is an outstanding person. It is a view that we will consider, along with many others.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister must know that it is not only George Ball who holds this view. I only quoted him because I thought the Prime Minister might have respected his opinion. May I then ask the Prime Minister directly, since the Minister of National Defence is keeping so quiet about this, if the Prime
Oral Questions
Minister believes that the whole star wars concept does undermine deterrence and changes the whole strategic doctrine? Does he share that view? Does he think the star wars concept has been ill-considered and ill-thought out? I would like to know upon what the Prime Minister bases his favourable view of star wars.

Mr. Speaker, I would just tell the Hon. Member that there are about half a dozen hypothetical questions locked into that one question. There is a position that the Secretary of State for External Affairs set out with great clarity and maturity on January 21 last, and it is the position of the Government. I suppose that if we were as sure as the Hon. Member opposite that there was no threat and no possibility of similar developments on the other side, we might be inclined to take a different view of certain developments. However, as the Secretary-General of NATO said, and the Hon. Member herself expressed respect for his view, it would be the height of imprudence not to proceed with research at this particular time.
We believe that there is a fundamental difference between the two sides. This one speaks to the moral issues of freedom, justice, and democracy, and that is where we stand. Those are the values that we will uphold while searching for a durable peace. The Hon. Member can be certain of that.
