speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to announce to the Hon. Members that the Government has reached an understanding with the Public Service unions on a number of issues that are important both to our employees and to the Treasury Board as the employer.
In recent months, I have had several meetings with union representatives to discuss these issues which had been pending for a number of years. The Government firmly believes that it must work together with the Public Service unions to get our economy going again and improve the standard of living of all Canadians, and it intends to succeed. It has always been our contention that the problems we are facing today can be solved. We know that our public administration must be made to function more effectively. We can improve it by making the Public Service more sensitive to the public's needs and also more effective. We can improve it by introducing new guidelines for co-operation, by holding consultations before making decisions and by setting common goals for settling important matters. The system adopted by this Government can serve as a model, and its aim is to create fair, effective and responsible labour-management relations in Canada.

As a result of the meetings which I held with Public Service union representatives, this Government has agreed to introduce in the Public Service a system of master agreement bargaining, a dental plan, a revised pension plan and improved workforce adjustment procedures.
On the issue of master agreement bargaining, I signed memoranda of understanding last week with representatives of the two major Public Service unions, the Public Service Alliance of Canada and the Professional Institute of the Public
April 17, 1985

Service of Canada. The memoranda provide terms of reference under which it will be possible to negotiate master agreements covering approximately 80 per cent of the terms and conditions of employment which are now found in individual collective agreements.
Under the present system, negotiated terms and conditions of employment are bargained for each bargaining unit represented by each union. Some of the terms and conditions are unique to a bargaining unit, but in many cases similar collective agreement articles can be found in many agreements, often using exactly the same language. Yet, until now, those articles had to be negotiated separately for each collective agreement. For example, in the case of the Alliance, they would be negotiated for each of the 39 collective agreements. Under the master agreement system, such articles would be negotiated only once with the Alliance at a master table.
The master agreement approach to collective bargaining is much more efficient. Not only will we be required to spend less time at the bargaining table, thereby ultimately reducing the cost of the bargaining process, but collective agreements will be easier to administer and interpret.
Any impasses at the master agreement bargaining table will be resolved through a process of binding conciliation. Thus, the right to strike will not apply to items which will be included in master agreements.

It will be impossible to negotiate all conditions at the master table, Mr. Speaker, owing to the diversity of professional groups in the Public Service. This difficulty is acknowledged in the concept of second tier bargaining where the collective agreements of professional groups will be negotiated on an individual basis so as to settle clearly monetary issues such as rate of pay, benefits, working hours and paid holidays.
The second tier-bargaining of individual collective agreements-will operate much as it does now and will include staggered expiry dates and recourse to binding arbitration or conciliation-strike in case of deadlock.
Since the Public Service Staff Relations Act now provides for bargaining units negotiating on an individual basis, it will have to be amended to implement the system of master agreement bargaining. Both parts will be more effective and enjoy more freedom of action to solve labour issues.
Mr. Speaker, the Public Service Staff Relations Act has practically remained unchanged since it came into effect in 1967, and the Government will hold consultations on this issue with labour representatives and other interested parties.
With respect to Public Service pensions, the Government believes that contributors to the Public Service pension plan should have their say in the decision-making process which leads eventually to the definition and administration of policy. We are quite agreeable to the establishment of a joint management system. The system provides for the creation of a management committee chaired by an independent person and will
Statement by Minister
be made up of at least twelve members representing the employer and the employees, on an equal basis. It will answer to me in my capacity as President of the Treasury Board. [English]
It is our intention to bring the Public Service pension schemes more in line with those in the private sector. As a result, and in response to concerns expressed by employees, the public sector and the Auditor General, we will fund and finance Public Service pension plans in accordance with the accepted practices and standards of the major employers in the private sector.
I would like to underline four points. The current indexing will be replaced by an inflation protection feature dependent upon the earnings of the fund. The management board will review contribution rates and the plan features periodically and recommend adjustments. Unfunded actuarial liabilities resulting from past practices will be amortized within the plan in an orderly fashion over a period of not less than 25 years. Under the new proposals, benefits will be funded in advance. The fund will not accumulate further actuarial deficits.
Finally, pension accounts will be credited with interest earnings based on returns achieved in a representative sample of private sector plans. In all other aspects the Public Service plans will, as a minimum, generally meet the requirements of the federal Pension Benefits Standards Act. These changes will require legislative amendments which will be brought before this House following further consultation with the advisory committee on the Public Service Superannuation Act.
On the subject of a Public Service dental plan, I have signed an agreement setting out the principles under which a moderate plan will be introduced. A board of trustees will be appointed consisting of an independent chairperson and equal representation from the unions and the employer. This board of trustees will be responsible for the sound financial administration of the plan, which is to be self-insured.
An agreement has been reached on improvements to the workforce adjustment policy. The Government's policy is that employees whose jobs are no longer required will, as far as possible, be redeployed within the Public Service with retraining, if necessary. Briefly, major improvements to the policy include; first, the minimum notice to an employee whose job is being abolished will be increased from three months to four months, although Departments will endeavour to give at least six months' notice. Second, laid off persons will be eligible for retraining, and those accepting lower level positions will be provided with up to one year's salary protection.
The understanding reached on these issues, Mr. Speaker, goes a long way toward fulfilling the promises we made last summer during the federal election campaign. Two other issues will require further consultation. I have already mentioned one, the amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. The other involves the political rights of public servants which need further careful consideration to ensure

April 17, 1985
Statement by Minister
fairness and equity to all concerned. I am confident that these matters will also be satisfactorily resolved.

Collective efforts have led to those achievements of which Canadians are proudest. This Government listens, consults, finds innovative solutions to national problems. Genuine efforts are made to achieve results. The Progressive Conservative Government will reach its targets and live up to its commitments, for it has every intention of calling upon Canadians to help it meet all challenges.
Mr. Speaker, the measures announced today are the starting point of a new era in the field of labour-management relations in the federal administration. Those issues had been upsetting labour-management relations for many years. Yet, in the short time since this Government took office, it has succeeded in bargaining in a spirit of co-operation and, in so doing, finding responsible solutions.
In that same spirit, Mr. Speaker, we will continue to be open about our concerns and to keep those of our employees in mind. In our opinion, the employees, the federal Government as employer, and the people of Canada all stand to benefit.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) on having provided us with a copy of his statement a few hours before it was presented in the House.
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is the employer that has the largest labour force in the country and it is therefore important, and even very important that the issues pertaining to the way the Government manages its human resources be discussed in this House, and if possible settled amicably.

There are four items in this statement, Mr. Speaker, which the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) addresses. I would just like to repeat them: the system of master agreement bargaining, a dental plan, a revised pension plan and improved workforce adjustment procedures.
The system of master agreement, of course, is the same as that which was called either a common language agreement or a master wording agreement when the previous administration was negotiating for an agreement on this matter. I do not think the semantics are very important. The fact is that the previous Liberal administration for years had been talking with the unions about this process and had come to a certain understanding. The apple was ripe, the Minister picked it and I congratulate him for doing so. I believe it is a step in the right direction. However, I would like to remind him that humility sometimes helps and that he has to agree that past Presidents of the Treasury Board did accomplish a lot of work on this matter. I congratulate also the unions. The important part of this agreement is their acceptance of this master agreement. I take some joy in congratulating the Minister on his success in
picking the apple, as I said, and bringing it forth in such a short time. The Minister talked about amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. I would imagine that he will be coming forth soon with the required amendments to put in force a master agreement bargaining process.
There are certain things that we have addressed over the years-and when I say "we" I mean this Parliament and the employee organizations-in trying to improve employer-employee relations. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the long discussions which were held in regard to the designation process of employees; who designates them, how many are going to be designated, and what is the process which is to be used. I believe that has been an important factor in years gone by in preventing what I would call "amicable relations" from existing between the Treasury Board as an employer and the unions. I hope that anything which is done in terms of a master agreement will encourage public servants and their representatives, the negotiating and bargaining agents, to take the route of arbitration, that is the binding arbitration route, rather than to choose the conciliation-strike route. That is, 1 suppose, the main purpose of my comments with regards to the master contract and the amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. There is nothing in this declaration today, Mr. Speaker, which would lead, at least the public servants or myself at this time, to think that we can read into this announcement anything that will accomplish this. So I hope that the Minister will keep in mind that what we actually look for is an improved negotiating atmosphere in public servants' relations through that designation process, which indeed, in my short time here, has been a thorn in the side of the unions, and justifiably so.
The second question, of course, deals with the dental plan. The Minister talked about a new moderate dental plan. This is something for which, indeed, the Public Service of Canada has been asking for a long time. This is a major announcement and it is welcomed by this Party. But, again, it would have been appreciated if we could have had more specific information. There are an awful lot of questions to be asked, and a major statement of this importance without any financial details appended thereto leaves one wondering about the financial implications. What are the modalities of its application? Who pays for what? Is it pay-as-you-go, cost sharing, voluntary or optional? I would have appreciated at least some ballpark figures from the Minister in terms of the financial commitment, who pays what and who gets what. Nevertheless, I would again like to congratulate the Government and the unions and I say that it is a step in the right direction.
Before I get to the third item, I understand there is to be a board of trustees, which is a nice way of administering such a dental plan. I take it it will be looking into the costs and contributions from members. But what does self-insured mean? What does it mean to public servants? There are all kinds of ways and means of addressing this question, but I will have to wait for the Minister to table further information.
April 17, 1985

The pension issue, of course, is something that I like, having had very deep involvement and interest in the matter over the years. I will not expand on that too much because 1 think Members of the House understand that I could probably take up the rest of the afternoon in talking about indexing of Public Service pensions and probably bore you all to death with the subject. But I am pleased to see that the current problems of the so-called pension funds are going to be addressed. 1 am somewhat mystified by the pay-as-you-go basis which the Minister is taking. What exactly does it mean to public servants in terms of their contributions? It will be interesting to study that matter with him in due course when he comes forward with the legislation amending the pension fund legislation. We will wait for it before congratulating the Minister because it is a real hornet's nest, and he knows it too, I think.

The pension plan management system is interesting. However, I have some doubts about it. For instance, the Minister has said that he will be responsible for the management committee, which will include one chairman and twelve directors, at least twelve directors as stated in the press release, which suggests that there will be fair and equitable representation from both sides to be chosen and appointed by the Minister or by Order in Council following consultations with the unions, or rather, this is not explained in the-
Six to be appointed by the employer and six by the unions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The Minister has specified that six will be appointed by the employer, that is the Government, and six by the unions. This is one thing that the unions will find satisfactory. In any case, they will have their say on how the plan will be administered.
Now we have to determine how the monies due to the pension plan will be contributed within less than 25 years. Will the indexation fund and the pension fund be put together? Will this huge amount of money, the billions of dollars invested in those funds, be used to finance the whole plan or will the funds remain separate? The pension fund has well above $20 billion, but the indexation fund, which of course was set up more recently, is smaller and is the one which most often creates the actuarial problems we have discussed many times in this House.
The fourth point is-

-the workforce adjustment policies. There is nothing very new in this except that I applaud the commitment made by the Government to retrain those people who, through no fault of their own, because of modernization, technological change, and economic adjustments have been laid off or asked to leave.
As to the four-month extension, well, most Departments had three months and were asked to grant six months, and so now we have four months and we are going to ask them for at least
Statement by Minister
six months. That is not a very big change but it is something in the bank and it will help public servants in adjusting to work changes in the Public Service.
The amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act are interesting. The House of Commons will recall that in 1976 a joint committee of this House and the Senate sat for close to a year and a half reviewing employer-employee relations in the Public Service of Canada following Jacob Finkelman's report to the House of Commons. 1 thought he did a very thorough and interesting study of this relationship. I would like to ask the Minister again to show celerity on this matter of bringing in amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. There are difficult problems at hand and 1 would like to see them resolved, so I am sure he can count on our support and co-operation in trying to come to grips with these amendments.

Concerning the promises made by the Government to the Public Service and the Canadian people during the electoral campaign, true enough, the Minister has kept four out of six of his own promises. This is a very good record, but the Minister has not dealt with the six or seven other interesting matters which were also the subject of promises. What about classification of positions, staffing, and a whole gamut of issues, such as technological changes, job designations which 1 mentioned earlier, and certain other things that are negotiable?
There certainly remains a lot to be done. The Minister will have a chance to examine these issues carefully and perhaps to propose changes shortly to render classification standards negotiable. In my opinion, this question is rather important at this time.
I therefore want to tell the Minister that he has shown that he is capable of doing something meaningful. We shall now see whether his legislation is adequate, and if I may speak for my colleagues in this House, I hope that the Minister will soon be in a position to introduce the amendments needed to implement the dental plan and bring about the required changes to the Act. If he has enough time, he may want to reply to some of the questions I have asked him.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this important announcement by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). I congratulate him, his officials and the Public Service union representatives who worked long and hard with the Minister and his staff since January in coming to agreement in four of the six important areas which were on the table at the commencement of the discussions. It is true that not every promise made by the Progressive Conservatives during the election has been fulfilled, and some have been forgotten. Therefore, there is absolutely no question that this announcement is welcomed. It is a very positive announcement for the 250,000 men and women who work for the people of Canada, and it is very

April 17, 1985
Statement by Minister
much, I believe, in the spirit of the commitment made by the Progressive Conservatives last year.
I recognize that there has been some give and take by the unions in their discussions with the Government. Specifically, in return for a master agreement, the unions have given up the right to strike regarding those items that are covered by the master agreement. These items will be refereed by a compulsory conciliation or arbitration process, and that is obviously a major concession on the part of the unions. I think they recognize that there were gains to be had, and I think that there are very positive gains in having common conditions for the most part for all people working in the Public Service of Canada.
I think it is important to free up the time of people who administer labour relations, both on the side of management of the civil service and on the side of public sector unions. If that time is used constructively I think it can lead to a much better climate for labour relations and to more positive and co-operative work arrangements. I think that is very important and I would like to see it copied in the private sector as well. This spirit is not entirely abroad in terms of labour management relations across the country.
The Minister is aware, for example, of the contrary position taken by the Governments of the Provinces of British Columbia and Quebec, both of which have acted to attempt to demean workers in the Public Service and to take their rights away. Those are very negative actions. In the private sector as well there have been many instances when employers have not been prepared to recognize the rights of workers to have unions and to participate in decisions. In effect, they have been trying to go back to the 19th century rather than to move forward into the 21st century.
I am sure the Minister is storing this up to be used perhaps in communications to his Party from time to time. I think it is fair to say that the proof of the pudding is in the eating. [Translation]
This will depend on the manner in which the promises are kept. The spirit of the agreement is quite positive, but we will have to wait and see how the agreements that have been promised as well as the four other points the Minister has mentioned are implemented.

We certainly hope and expect that this will be carried out in the same spirit. I would personally like to congratulate the Minister because I think he has probably had something of a sticky wicket in terms of dealing with members of the senior civil service who were perhaps not totally in accord with what the Minister was putting forward in seeking to implement promises made by his Party last summer. I would ask those senior civil service employees who have to negotiate the agreements to recognize that at least two Parties in the House of Commons are very much committed to what the Minister has said today.
With regard to the Liberal Party, I welcome the comments of my friend from Ottawa-Vanier. It is true that while they were in power since 1968 they had the chance to bring in a dental plan, but they resisted it. They had the chance to move to a master agreement, but they refused to go along with that. They had the chance to reform pension arrangements, but they did not do it. If they have come around to that point of view now, I welcome that. I certainly hope that people in the Public Service recognize that there is a very strong political commitment to have these things translated into specific actions.
When the Minister sat down with the unions in January there were six different areas of concern. One of the areas not yet resolved is that of political rights. The Minister is confident that this matter "will be satisfactorily resolved". He states that the question of political rights "needs careful consideration to ensure fairness and equity to all concerned".
As the Minister knows, on Monday I initiated a debate on this particular question in the House of Commons. I initiated it because of my commitment and that of my Party to the question of winning political rights for people working for the Public Service of Canada. I was pleased to hear the positive comments of government Members such as the Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick), the Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister (Mr. Lewis), as well as the positive comments of my friend, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier).
1 understand that some 50 Members of Parliament have now indicated in writing to the Public Service Alliance that they endorse the positions taken in favour of political rights by their respective Parties. Last summer, in response to the Alliance, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated quite explicitly that the Progressive Conservatives favour a general removal of the restrictions on political activity, especially for those public servants who are covered by collective agreements. Perhaps the Minister will agree with me that in the spirit of what is being done today we can, in the future, refer to the people working for the Public Service of Canada as public sector workers rather than public servants, which may have a demeaning connotation. They are workers who do a very important job.
The excellent t.v. advertisements which have been put out by the Alliance over the last month or so have been surprising and positive for people in the country. They showed the range of occupations of Public Service employees working for the people of Canada. They are meteorologists, truck drivers, coast guards and those who do scientific work. It is certainly a far cry from the image of public employees as parasites drawing fancy salaries and sitting in fancy offices in Ottawa effectively doing nothing but conspiring to learn how they can get their next promotion. There may be one or two people like that, as there are in any organization, Mr. Speaker. However, the skill, commitment and engagement of the people who work for the people of Canada as public sector employees should be commended in the House of Commons in this particular discussion. I think it is reflected in what the Minister has done today.
April 17, 1985

However, public sector employees are not equal with regard to the question of political rights. The Minister's statement comes on the day when the equality section of the Charter has come into force. I hope that he will indicate today that he is now prepared, on behalf of the Government, to commit the Government to providing political rights to make public sector employees equal to all other Canadians.
While speaking in the debate on Monday I suggested very specifically that all people working for the Public Service of Canada who are in bargaining units-which would include over 200,000 of our public sector employees-should enjoy political rights on the same basis as all other Canadians, except perhaps with respect to the specific areas in which they are engaged. I suggested that the exclusion from political activity should only apply to the very senior civil service workers. There should perhaps be a system of qualified rights, as suggested in the D'Avignon report, for those management employees who are not in bargaining units but who are not in the top mandarin positions. In that case we may need a case-by-case means of determining which of those persons should have political rights and which should not.
People who ran in the federal election by taking leave from the Public Service were allowed to take leave, stand as candidates, and return to their former jobs in most cases without a political taint accompanying the fact that they were candidates for a particular political Party. Given those circumstances, I find it hard to understand why we cannot allow those public sector employees to enjoy full political rights. Their votes indicate that many of them support my Party, many support the Liberal Party, and a substantial number support the Progressive Conservative Party. In other words, public sector employees are a mirror of the country. By allowing a group of people who mirror the country to enjoy political rights we will not undermine impartiality.
With regard to specifics, we welcome the dental plan which had been so short-sightedly rejected by the Liberals. We will have to study the details, but it will certainly be welcomed by large numbers of people working in the Public Service. We welcome the new arrangement with respect to the pension plan provisions. I hope that the provisions for joint management will spread to the private sector. I would welcome legislation being put forward by one of the Minister's colleagues requiring that that be done with respect to pension plans in the private sector.
I would like to remind the Minister of the concerns of retirees about their pensions being rolled back under the six and five program of the previous Government. That represents a loss of an average of $1,000 a year for the superannuated federal Government employees. I hope that before the new regime comes into effect the Government will act in order to restore the base and indexation that were lost by those particular employees so that it will not be a lifetime loss.
In conclusion I would like to speak on the question of workforce redeployment. I hope that the retraining facilities and the management of lay-offs will be considered much more
Statement by Minister
seriously than they have been in the past. I will comment on that later.
Finally, I hope that this does not represent a carrot on the stick and that the Budget and the Nielsen committee do not crack down on the public sector employees after what has been achieved today. I want to assure the Minister that if the Government plans to take after it has given, we will fight all the way and stand up for those public sector employees against arbitrary cuts and lay-offs. That being said, I welcome the announcement made today.
Questions?

Mr. Speaker, I have some rather specific questions. My first question concerns political rights. Is the Minister prepared to undertake now that in principle the Government will at least provide virtually full political rights to all public sector employees in the Government of Canada who are members of bargaining units, recognizing that there may be some difficulty in defining what political rights may be provided to personnel in management categories?

Mr. Speaker, I would have been the happiest person in the House had I been able to announce today an agreement and the resolution of all six issues that we have been discussing with the unions in such a co-operative and consultative fashion over the last six months.
As I mentioned today, we have reached agreement on four issues. One remaining issue concerns the PSSRA amendments which are more detailed and specific and take longer to negotiate. There is nothing ideological about that issue.
The other issue concerns a more difficult question. Even my hon. colleague, in his statement, raised a number of questions about how one defines certain things. All that I can assure my hon. friend is that discussions on this issue are under way. It is our commitment to pursue those discussions with the representatives of our various labour movements.
With respect to the question of political rights for public servants, as well as the amendments, globally, to the PSSRA, hopefully I will be in a position to make a statement in the House as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, in responding to the Public Service Alliance last summer, the Prime Minister stated that the Progressive Conservative Party favours a general removal of the restrictions to political activity, especially for those public sector workers who are covered by collective agreements. That is essentially what I was talking about.
Can we expect legislation that would essentially implement that commitment by the Progressive Conservatives during the election campaign before the House rises for the summer recess on June 28?

Mr. Speaker, once again, I would have been very happy to announce something today. It is an issue that is
3824

April 17, 1985
Statement by Minister
under active consideration by Government and by the representatives of all our public sector unions.
I believe that after having dealt successfully and very cooperatively on the first four issues, we will be able to do the same with the other issues.
The Hon. Member is asking me to give a definite date. I cannot give my hon. colleague a definitive date. All I can assure him of is that the fact that this was not announced today should not be seen as any indication that the Government does not accord this issue a high priority. It is just a matter of discussions and of reaching a mutual understanding with our colleagues on the labour side. This will continue very actively. What I have announced today is not the end but the beginning on a new era in labour relations.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the question of pensions, will the Minister undertake to supply both opposition Parties with the necessary documentation to study the subject matter so that we can understand and discuss this matter openly and also talk about the same questions?
As he knows, there are actuarial considerations and other economic factors involved in the whole question of pensions. It is an important subject and one which is very confusing. In order to allow time for us to look into it, will he give us the benefit of the information he has before him so that we can deal with it?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to provide the House with all the necessary information on this issue. I have indicated today the major principles on which the employer and employee representatives have reached an agreement. Of course, there remain many details which will have to be finalized. A number of actuarial studies will have to be completed. But as soon as representatives from both sides have negotiated and approved the last details, I will be pleased to table them in the House for all to see and make appropriate comments. There are no problems.

Mr. Speaker, I have two questions. I have a Private Members' Bill on the Order Paper, with respect to political nights, and there is an amendment by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) which says that the Bill be not now read a second time but the subject matter be referred to the appropriate committee of the House. Would the Minister prevail upon his House Leader to agree that that matter be called again and dealt with without further debate, in order that the subject matter of the Bill be referred to the appropriate committee, thus providing a vehicle for the Government and the Public Service unions to make their views known?
Second, does the Minister propose to continue the option of the right to strike, or will there be compulsory arbitration? Which route will he take?

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the first question, I am well aware of the Hon. Member's views with regard to referring this issue to a parliamentary committee. It is certainly something that I am more than happy to consider. However, I do take some objection to his suggestion that this would be necessary in order to provide a vehicle so that views can be made known. We have a vehicle which today has produced four very major amendments to the way we deal with labour-management relations.
I am trying to be helpful.

I appreciate that. That is why I am saying that in view of the Hon. Member's attempt to be helpful I will consider his point of view. I would like to pursue all the other methods of resolving this complex issue. We want it resolved and I believe that we are all working toward the same goal.
It is certainly something that I will consider and I will attempt to respond to the Hon. Member shortly on which way we would prefer to proceed.
The second point raised by the Hon. Member concerns the right to strike. It is not a question of giving up the right to strike or taking away the right to strike. I do not think that is an issue. We are essentially saying that the new scheme of bargaining at the master table was accepted mutually and was not something imposed by the Government. It was a question of both parties arriving at a mutually agreeable solution as to how to resolve an impasse should it arise at the master table. It is not arbitration, it is binding conciliation.
Perhaps I can give the Hon. Member some details about the way it would work. Rather than arbitration, there would be a system of binding conciliation whereby both the union involved, be it PIPS or PSAC, would appoint a conciliator and management would appointment a conciliator. They would be asked to agree jointly on an independent chairperson within a given period of time yet to be determined. Should those two appointed members, one from labour and one from management, not reach agreement within that time period, the chairperson would then be appointed by the chairman of the PSSRB.
Why not by you?

No, then it becomes too one-sided. I am sorry, but I think a fair deal has to be a fair deal. At that point, obviously, if the three agree it is binding. If there is a majority agreement it is binding. If the three agree to disagree, the chairperson's decision is the one that is binding on all parties.
From a legislative point of view, that is a very significant departure from the arbitration process we now have, because it gives a much more direct say to labour and to the employer in the selection of a panel.

A very short question, Mr. Speaker. Could the Minister indicate whether there is a time schedule for
April 17, 1985

implementing the four points he has mentioned today? Is there one for possible amendments? Will it take place during this session? Will it be completed within the present session? Can we expect the Minister to give us information about the dental plan? In other words, could the minister give us an idea of the time schedule agreed upon with the unions?

Mr. Speaker, when our negotiations started with labour associations, I expected that an agreement in principle would be reached for Easter. It was reached on Easter Monday; we unfortunately missed our goal by a day.
Obviously, it will take time to put into law what I announced today, and there will be unavoidable delays that should be respected in the House. For example, when we refer to the master agreement, the legislation must be amended and I think that it is useless to present only amendments concerning the master agreement when there is a long list of changes which are now being negotiated on other issues already mentioned by my colleague.
That is why we would like to introduce a series of amendments to the legislation. In the meantime, with respect to the master agreement, if my legal advice is correct, under a joint agreement with the unions, we can negotiate on that basis just the same. The unions have accepted the principle which must be ratified under the agreement and are willing, despite any amendment to the legislation, to proceed quickly with the negotiations on the master agreement.
The dental plan does not give rise to any legal problem, so we will carry on. It is merely a matter of mechanism to be determined.
As for adjustments to the labour force, they have already been approved and no amendment to the legislation is necessary; some change is needed but with agreement it could be done immediately. This means that pensions will be the issue which will require more consideration on the legislative level.
A calendar ? I should like of course to introduce a bill as soon as possible. Some actuarial studies will be done by both parties to enable us to come to an agreement about the provisions of the bill, but I surely hope that a bill will be introduced before the end of this session.

There have been consultations between the Parties. If Your Honour places this matter before the House, there will be a disposition to accept the following motion:

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Minister of Transport) moved:
subsubtopic: CNR PENSIONS-MOTION TO REFER TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Transport be empowered to study all matters related to the Canadian National Railways' pension system;
That the Committee have the power to retain expert, professional, technical and clerical staff.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak to the proposed order of reference and the amendment to which all the Parties unanimously agreed. The issue relates to the terms of reference with respect to CN pensions. I know many Hon. Members who have been in the House for quite some time have a particular interest in this issue, as do I. It has been around for a long time. I know they share a concern for the inadequacy of pensions for CN retirees. I think I can say quite safely that this extends beyond the ambit of CNR. Perhaps it would be more proper to address this question both to CN and to CP. Since CN is a Crown corporation, we have a responsibility to try to examine this issue in detail and, hopefully, reach a satisfactory conclusion.
It is in that spirit that I look forward to the comments of members of the New Democratic Party and of the Liberal Party. I am confident that they will find support for this measure and I hope that they will be able to support the reference. It is an issue which affects some 47,000 CN pensioners. Perhaps the implications will apply to other railway pensioners as well; let us hope so.
The Government is committed to ensuring that the matter of CN pensions receives the appropriate consideration of the Parliament of Canada. 1 say that because, as I indicated earlier, Members on all sides of the House for many years have had an abiding interest in this. There are Members here today who have participated in this issue before the standing committee. There have been many inquiries, such as the Hall inquiry on railway pensions in the mid-seventies and there was work following that.
April 17, 1985

I believe it is fair to say that Members have pursued this issue with a great amount of sincerity. We are trying to capitalize on that goodwill and sincerity to try and reach a fair and equitable solution by having this matter referred to the Standing Committee on Transport. I believe that the Standing Committee on Transport is really the appropriate vehicle to examine this issue. It is the appropriate forum for a number of reasons. First, it is a parliamentary body. I believe the committee will ensure that there are proper public hearings, which I believe is one of the things that is uppermost in the minds of pensioners. Representations that I have received indicate that the pensioners want the opportunity to discuss this issue in a public forum. They want the opportunity to present their concerns and grievances, and to hear the response of CN in front of their elected representatives in a duly constituted public forum. That is very important.
We on this side of the House believe that it is incumbent upon us to provide them with that opportunity. While there are some spokesmen from the Liberal Party, not necessarily in this Chamber today, who might take exception to the forum, I believe it is fair to say that the pensioners have recommended this kind of forum. I was pleased to note that in a CP article just recently Mr. J. Earl White, who has been referred to as the champion of the railway pensioners, said he was very encouraged by the action that the Government was taking. He is the head of the Vancouver based Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association. He retired in 1974 after 46 years of railway service and has been in the forefront of the battle for better pensions ever since. The article reads:
He said in a telephone interview he asked Mazankowski for the committee study because the issue has been studied enough by outside experts .... Mazankowski understands the issue and will understand the committee's recommendation, White said, adding the committee study is needed to clear away any doubts of how the national railways have abused their employees' pension plan.
I cite that not only because he says some very flattering words about yours truly, but as well because we have captured the essence of what the pensioners want. I think they are pleased with the forum that we are proposing here today.
As I said earlier, we believe that this is the right forum. We know that there was an inquiry proposed by the last administration. It was in recognition of these representations that I felt that the inquiry that was proposed by the previous administration would not necessarily meet the concerns of the pensioners. Therefore, we decided to cancel the inquiry that was set up by the previous Government.
I want to say to all Members of the House, and indeed to Mr. Brian Williams, that in making the decision I certainly in no way want to cast any reflection upon the integrity, reputation or ability of the commissioner who was appointed, namely Mr. Brian Williams of Vancouver. My decision to cancel that procedure should in no way be construed as a reflection upon his competence, but rather it was a decision based upon the desire to proceed in a more direct public manner in tune with the issues and the desires of the pensioners, the people who feel
Canadian National Pensions
aggrieved by the way in which their pensions had been handled.
The second reason for choosing the Standing Committee on Transport is that, as well as being a pension issue, this is a matter which involves Canada's railways. There has always been a special relationship in Canada between the railways and Parliament. I think that is recognized by the fact that we have a Railway Committee Room in this building. The Railway Committee Room stands as the permanent room for the activities of the Standing Committee on Transport.
Those of us who have been a part of this committee for many years are very proud of that fact. I guess that in a technical sense I am not a member of that committee, but I still feel very much a part of it.

subsubtopic: CNR PENSIONS-MOTION TO REFER TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is still your home.

subsubtopic: CNR PENSIONS-MOTION TO REFER TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, I feel very much at home when I go to meetings of the standing committee. The railways have a special place in the history of our country. I believe that the people who work for the railways deserve special recognition.
I know that in my days as a member of the standing committee, the concerns of railway employees were always of interest and concern to all members who sat on that committee, particularly those who were former railroaders and never ceased their efforts on behalf of their co-workers.
I can certainly single out the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), who has been a champion on behalf of not only the current railway workers, but of the pensioners; his former colleague from Moose Jaw, Mr. Skoberg; and, of course, the eminent Member of the other place, the former Whip of the Liberal Party, Senator Charlie Turner, who certainly distinguished himself in terms of representing the interests of the railway workers and pensioners. I guess if I had one regret, it is that Mr. Turner will not be a member of that committee. I am sure that he will find the occasion to come in from time to time and give the committee any advice it may wish to extract from him.
I am sure as well that the present committee will benefit from many of the new members. The new membership on that committee is made up of a very talented group of Canadians. That new blood and expertise, combined with the stability, wisdom and commitment of veterans like the chief spokesman for the Official Opposition Party and the chief spokesman for the New Democratic Party and others, that blend will augur well in coming up with a real set of balanced recommendations that we can follow.
I urge all Members of the House and the standing committee to remember that we are dealing with an issue that affects the lives of some 47,000 former CN employees and their dependants. It may very well have implications beyond that. These people have provided years of dedicated service to our country, many for as long as 30 or 40 years. They are now senior citizens and do not have the sophisticated computers or lawyers to argue their case. I believe that their views must be

April 17, 1985
Canadian National Pensions
heard and that in the standing committee they will find a responsive and sympathetic listener.
Third, and this relates to my previous comments, the standing committee has shown considerable interest in this matter in the past and has acquired a knowledge and understanding that should be utilized. As recently as in the spring of 1984, the standing committee was seized with this particular issue. The committee had the opportunity, at least in part, to hear from the Pensioners' Association and CN. Unfortunately, we were not able to complete a thorough examination such as today we are proposing to do.
Previous to that in June, 1982 the standing committee adopted the motion of the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) to consider the issue. Regrettably, that examination was also not concluded. Given the historical work of the committee, its interest in railway issues and the desire of the pensioners for a proper public hearing, I think that the broad order of reference to the committee which we have put forward is the most appropriate approach to this long-standing and very complex matter.
I must emphasize that the decision to bring forward an order of reference is consistent with the Government's interest in an over-all approach to Canada's pension and retirement income system. We are fully aware of the importance of the whole pension question and the great deal of work and examination that has been undertaken recently. Our Government is committed to assisting all Canadians in preparing for retirement that would allow them to live in dignity and security. I believe that the efforts of the Standing Committee on Transport with respect to CN pensions will provide valuable information and insight regarding retirement income arrangements for all Canadians.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House by discussing the specific issues of concern to the pensioners. I believe we should leave it to the wisdom of the committee to determine the best manner in which to proceed on those questions which might require special attention. We deliberately tried to shape the order of reference to permit this sort of flexibility. At the same time, notwithstanding the committee's own expertise, we have recognized that this issue contains many complex technical, legal and financial elements. Accordingly, we believe that the committee will benefit from the assistance of various experts such as actuaries and pension fund analysts, and that the terms of reference provide the committee with the ability to engage such assistance as it may require. Again, that expertise and background competence that will be required combined with the expertise and the political judgment of the members of the committee will, I am sure, give us the ingredients to come forth with what I would hope to be fair, equitable and practical recommendations.
If I might, I would like to say that I think this reflects the kind of faith that we as a Government place in the institutions and instruments of Parliament, and that faith is shared by all Members on this side of the House. We are committed to
restoring the role of Parliament and parliamentarians and in particular we believe that committees can play a valuable role in the exploration of issues and the formulation of public policy. I say to the members of the Standing Committee on Transport that I intend to seek their advice on a wide range of issues and policy matters. I hope to count upon their advice and good counsel on these issues. They have already provided valuable advice and recommendations in several areas and I look forward to their efforts with regard to the CN pensions and to other matters.
If I may indulge in a moment of flattery, I would like to state that in my years as a parliamentarian, there has been no finer committee in the House than the Standing Committee on Transport. I have witnessed, as I am sure have many Hon. Members, some very remarkable and fascinating debates around that committee table. A great deal of thoughtful analysis has provided many outstanding and constructive reports and pieces of legislation to this House. I know that that tradition will be hard to live up to, but I am confident that the present membership is equal to that task. I sincerely look forward to their positive efforts on behalf of CN's 47,000 pensioners and I urge the House to give its approval to the order of reference so that the committee can get down to work.

subsubtopic: CNR PENSIONS-MOTION TO REFER TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to support a motion presented by the Government on behalf of my Party, the Liberal Party of Canada, a motion that will empower the Standing Committee on Transport to study the very important question of the Canadian National Railways' pension plan. It is a question that, as the Minister said earlier, affects some 45,000 CN pensioners, and as such, it is extremely important but also extremely complex and should be examined forthwith by the Members of this House, since it has already been the subject of discussions and in-depth studies for a number of years. These pensioners want action, and they want that action to be taken as soon as possible in this case.
I noticed that the Minister said the motion will empower committee members to retain the services of experts, professional technical staff, actuaries and other professionals to help them in their work. The Minister has therefore realized that this is a very complex matter. In fact, although I can give the House the assurance that the Members of the Official Opposition are prepared to give their full co-operation and support for this study, there are nevertheless two things that I regret. First of all, I think this Government has taken far too long since the opening of the new session to decide what it was going to do, before it finally referred this question to the Standing Committee on Transport. It is a decision I can accept, and I congratulate the Minister for having made the decision. However, I would have preferred the Committee to have been better prepared to do its work. The Minister mentioned earlier that he had to cancel a study by an expert who had been selected to examine the question by the previous, Liberal, Government. 1 maintain that if the study by this independent expert had been done, the Members of the Standing Committee who must examine this matter today would have been better prepared to do their work quickly, incisively and effectively.
I think it would be in order to recall a few historical facts. The Minister mentioned the name of Mr. Earl White, the National President of the Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association. The House will recall that Mr. White appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport on June 7, 1984. I am going to quote a short passage from the statement made by Mr. White at that time. He said that they examined the pensions being paid by the CN pension fund and concluded that CN were using an inappropriate or unsound mathematical equation to calculate pensions. This had led to massive gains to the fund at the expense of pensioners.
Mr. White went on to say in his statement before the Standing Committee on Transport, and I quote:
Canadian National Pensions
CN chose to use an inappropriate equation and have continued to use it for 19 years of highcr-than-normal inflation. As a result, it is estimated that about 20 per cent of the pension that pensioners should have received has stayed in the fund. Some pensioners will receive in 1984 only about half the pension they should receive. Others will receive about 17 per cent more than they should receive, but that is a short-term gain.

Mr. Speaker, this was indeed a very serious charge which caused some commotion among members of the Standing Committee on Transport.
Following Mr. White's testimony, the President of Canadian National, Dr. Maurice LeClair, wrote a letter to the Minister of Transport at the time in which he made the following comments, which I also would like to quote very briefly. Mr. LeClair said the following, and I quote:

The most recent evidence of this concern is a submission presented to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport by the President of the Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association, Mr. J. Earl White. The Association's brief was provided to the Committee members on 28 May, and Mr. White appeared as a witness before the Committee on 7 June.
We are prepared to appear before the Standing Committee to respond to the statements made in the brief and to answer any other questions concerning the Company's management of its pension plans.
However, it seems to me that the interests of all parties involved in this debate would be better served by some new initiative designed to remove the mistrust which appears to exist at the present time.
I am suggesting that you consider the appointment of an independent consultant or advisor to review CN's stewardship of its pension plans and pension trust fund and report to you on his/her findings. The examination should include an analysis of the matters contained in the submission presented to the Parliamentary Committee by Mr. White on behalf of the Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association.
At the same time, we believe it would be useful to report on the adequacy of the ad hoc adjustments provided to our pensioners. It is our opinion that our actions in this regard should be assessed in comparison with other "commercial" Crown corporations and large private sector employers, especially those of our main competitor, and with appropriate recognition to the level of initial benefit provided by our pension plans and the ratio of pensioners to active members of our workforce.

Subsequently, after hearing these widely divergent points of view, the Minister of Transport appointed on August 21, 1984, Mr. Bryan Williams of Vancouver as special adviser responsible for examining the financing and administration of Canadian National's pension plan. This independent commissioner could obtain the views of both parties and be instrumental in neutralizing the atmosphere of suspicion that seemed to prevail on both sides, and he would be able to review the structure, policy and administration of CN pension plans as well as the pension fund itself. The commissioner was to include a detailed analysis of the claims presented by the Pensioners' Association before the Standing Committee on Transport on May 28, 1984. He was to have meetings with most of the parties concerned in this case, including CN authorities, the Pensioners' Association, the unions, government representatives and pensions experts. Everyone had

April 17, 1985
Canadian National Pensions
approved and applauded this initiative by the Minister of Transport at the time. Everyone acknowledged the competence and impartiality of the expert in question, and 1 was glad to hear the Minister earlier this afternoon when he recognized the qualifications and impartiality of Mr. Williams, whose competence and ability to examine such issues are certainly not in doubt. In fact, Mr. Williams had already started on his study. He had several meetings with the President of Canadian National and his immediate staff. He also met with union representatives and already started to do some very important and very useful work. All of a sudden, however, he received a letter, a notice, a telex in fact, announcing that his services were no longer required by the new Minister of Transport.
1 think this was a rather hasty decision on the part of the new Minister, because it will cause the Members who are to examine this question to lose more time. The fact that the Minister, in his motion, recommends retaining the services of consultants, actuaries and specialists to help Members in the work they will have to do in the weeks to come clearly indicates how important it would be to have this impartial, independent and objective study to give Members some clarification regarding the recommendations and the decisions they will have to make. 1 say that if Mr. Williams had been allowed to continue his work, we would now, on this very day, have a thorough study of the issues that would help us understand and analyze what we can and what we should decide on the Standing Committee on Transport. And we would not have to start from scratch as will now probably be the case, and hear testimony and get the advice and information of all parties concerned, consult the experts and finally make recommendations. All this work would have been done in recent months, and we would now, in Committee, have been able to proceed with an analysis of the expert's recommendations after examining any testimony he would have been able to collect, and in a few weeks we would have been able to proceed and give satisfaction to the parties concerned.
1 believe that the task that awaits the Committee on Transport is a very difficult one that will take several weeks and that will require a great deal of attention and a great deal of study on the part of the members of this Committee. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal Members who sit on the committee will be unremitting and unrelenting in their work on behalf of those pensioners, for it is obvious that we consider this to be a vital matter for thousands of CN pensioners who have been urging all along that something be done about it. I give them the assurance that we will give our undivided attention to this new mandate of the Standing Committee on Transport.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, we fully support the motion, but we believe that the work will take more time and be more difficult because Mr. Bryan Williams was not allowed to do the preliminary work required to find acceptable solutions to this problem. I hope we come up with the answers
and find a satisfactory solution to this question of retired CN workers' pensions. The recommendations of the Standing Committee on Transport will also be useful to Canadian Pacific pensioners because, although the Canadian National is a Crown corporation and our duty is to look after Government employees or CN pensioners, I would suggest that our work will serve the interests of CP pensioners. That is the hope I express, Mr. Speaker, as I give you the assurance that the representatives of the Official Opposition will do their utmost to find a viable solution to this problem.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot let the observations and intervention by the transport critic of the Official Opposition go by without at least a brief comment. The distinguished Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) should know better than to attempt to mislead this chamber and the pensioners. The Hon. Member for Papineau is fully aware that this matter was before the Standing Committee as early as 1982. The committee at that time was prepared to go ahead with it. The then Minister of Transport was not prepared to let us go ahead, and I can assume that was because of a government decision.
The second comment I would like to make is, the Hon. Member will be fully aware that it was in early November when the first draft of the terms of reference for this very matter with which we are dealing today was presented to the Official Opposition for its consideration. It was rejected at that time by the House Leader of the Official Opposition and by the transport critic.
My third brief comment has to do with the single commissioner named by the former Minister of Transport. When was he named and under what circumstances? It was in the heat of an election in response to pressures being brought to bear upon him, when, Mr. Speaker, in fact that Party had two and a half years to deal with it. It had been aware of the issue for four or five years. I have no specific questions to ask the Hon. Member, but I wanted the record very clear with respect to that matter. Don't start us out this way. We have a good committee. Perhaps if I have a question for the distinguished Hon. Member, it would be to ask whether or not his views could lead the committee to believe that he might grace the meetings once in a while with his presence.

subsubtopic: CNR PENSIONS-MOTION TO REFER TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In connection with the comments the Parliamentary Secretary has just made, I should like to say very briefly that the representations made last November to the House Leader of the Official Opposition clearly referred to the vast number of subcommittees which the government wanted to establish to meet the aspirations and frustrations of its crushing majority of backbenchers which it wanted to keep busy. Neither the House Leader of the Official Opposition nor the House Leader of the New Democratic Party could accept
April 17, 1985

the large number of subcommittees the government was recommending.
We received only recently its recommendation to refer the matter to a standing committee, not a special committee or a subcommittee, and we accepted it immediately.
Also, the Hon. Member has regards for no comments but his own. I have listened to him most attentively and I should appreciate it if he acted likewise.
Finally, he stated that Mr. Williams had been appointed during the election campaign. Let me tell him this: The impartiality and competence of the independent expert who was appointed at the time by the former Minister of Transport were recognized by all interested parties. Because the appointment of this highly qualified expert took place during the election campaign, the Parliamentary Secretary feels it is a political one.
So I understand why the new Minister of Transport has hurriedly cancelled that appointment which he considered a political one. I think it is regrettable, notwithstanding the fact that the appointment took place last August, during the election campaign. Mr. Speaker, the fact is that if he had not been fired by the new minister, Mr. Williams would probably have already completed his study, informed us of the results of his investigations and conversations with CN pensioners and officials, as well as with union representatives and Canadian pension plans administrators. But someone else will have to do that job all over again. I suggest, therefore, that the new Minister of Transports' ill-advised decision will only delay the work which, I think, we are all anxious to start.
